*When longing for them has overwhelmed me, the nun has cast down its pouring tears.*

Whoever says it is the name of the fish makes "the pen" the pen which God created and commanded to write down all existing things, and makes the pronoun in "they inscribe" refer to the angels. Whoever says "Nun" is the name of the inkwell makes "the pen" the pen commonly known in people's hands; Ibn ʿAbbas explicitly stated this, and makes the pronoun in [p. 365] ﴿they inscribe﴾ refer to people. In this case the oath comes by the whole matter of writing, which is the foundation of the sciences, knowledge, and the affairs of this world and the Hereafter, for the pen is the brother of the tongue, the mount of intelligence, and a general blessing from God, the Exalted. Muʿawiyah ibn Qurrah related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Nun is a tablet of light." Ibn ʿAbbas and others also said: "Nun" is one of the letters of al-Rahman (the Most Merciful). They said: it has been separated in the Qur'an into "Alif-Lam-Ra," "Ha-Mim," and "Nun."

ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read, with a variant, "Nūna" in the accusative, meaning: "Mention Nun." This is strengthened by the possibility that it is the name of the surah. It is feminine, and a feminine name was given to it, so it has both femininity and definiteness, and for this reason it is not declined. "Nuh" is declined because its lightness, being three letters, overcame the cause of non-Arabic origin. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq, and al-Hasan read "Nūni" with a kasra on the nun, and this is like what you say in an oath: "Allah." As they said "Jayr." It was also said that it was given a kasra because two unvowelled letters came together. Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, and Hafs from ʿAsim read "Nūn" with a sukun (unvowelled) nun. This is on the basis that it is a separate letter, so it must be paused upon. A group, including al-Kisai, read "Nun, by the pen" with idgham (assimilation) without ghunnah (nasalization). Others read with idgham and with ghunnah. Al-Kisai, Yaʿqub, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read with ikhfa' (concealment), between idgham and izhar (clear pronunciation). "Yasturuna" means: they write lines. If God intends the angels, it is the recording of deeds and what they are commanded. If He intends the children of Adam, it is the revealed books, the sciences, and what is similar to them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ is the answer to the oath. Here "ma" is operative, having a subject and a predicate, and likewise when the preposition "bi" enters the predicate. His saying, the Exalted, "by the grace of your Lord," is a parenthetical insertion, as you say to a man: "You are, praise be to God, excellent."

The cause of this verse is that the Quraysh accused the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of madness, which is the covering of the intellect, meaning that his speech was erroneous like the speech of a madman. God, the Exalted, negated this from him, informed him that he has a reward, and that he is upon a great character, as an honor and praise to him.

People differed about the meaning of "maMnūn" (cut off). Most exegetes said: it is the weak and cut off; it is said "a rope mamnūn," that is, weak. Others said its meaning is: not reckoned against you, that is, not burdened by whoever is with you. Mujahid said its meaning is: not counted and not reckoned in a limited sense, that is, without account. [p. 366] ʿĀʾishah, may God be pleased with her, was asked about the character of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and she said: "His character was the Qur'an," meaning his manners and his commands. ʿAli, may God be pleased with him, said: The great character is the manners of the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, expressed "character" as religion and the law, and this is without doubt the head and foundation of character. Yet the apparent meaning of the verse is that the creation is what opposes the disbelievers' intent in their saying "madman," that is, one who does not have sound grasp of what he says. Indeed God praised him for noble disposition, excellence of nature, a fine temperament, and good qualities. From this is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "I was sent to complete the noble characteristics," and Junayd said: "His character was called great because he had no aspiration other than God, the Exalted. He associated with creation by his character and was separated from them by his heart, so his outward was with creation and his inward was with the Truth." In the advice of some sages: "Upon you is good conduct with creation, and truthfulness with the Truth, and good character is entirely good." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed the believer reaches by his good character the rank of one who stands in prayer at night and fasts by day." And he said: "Nothing is heavier in the balance than good character." And he said: "The dearest of you to God are those with the best character." Justice, kindness, forgiveness and maintaining ties are all part of character.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So you will see﴾ means: you and your community. ﴿And they will see﴾ means: they. People differed about the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Which of you is the afflicted?﴾ Abu ʿUthman al-Mazini said: the sentence is complete at ﴿and they will see﴾, then He began again with ﴿Which of you is the afflicted?﴾ Al-Akhfash said: rather, the seeing operates on the interrogated clause in its meaning. As for the "bi" (in "bi-ayyikum"), Abu ʿUbaydah Maʿmar and Qatadah said it is superfluous, and the meaning is: "Which of you is the afflicted?" Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: "al-maftun" is in the sense of "fitnah" (affliction), as they say: "He has no ʿaql (intellect)," meaning no intellect; and as they say: "Accept his easy portion and leave his difficult portion." So the meaning is: which of you is the affliction and corruption that they called madness? Others said the meaning is: by which of you was the afflicted one afflicted? Al-Akhfash said the meaning is: by which of you is the affliction of the afflicted? Then the first noun was omitted and the second was put in its place. Mujahid and al-Farra' said: the "bi" means "fi" (in), that is: in which group among you is the afflicted kind? This is a good saying with little artificiality, and we do not say that one particle has the meaning of another; rather we say this meaning is reached by "fi" and also by "bi." Ibn Abi ʿAblah read: "Fi ayyikumu al-maftun."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾ to the end of the verse, is a warning. The governing element for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿of who has strayed﴾ is "most knowing," and the preposition has strengthened it, so it does not need a supposed verb. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not obey the deniers﴾ refers to the Quraysh, because they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at some times: "If you worship our gods and honor them, we will worship your God and honor Him." They wished that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would flatter them and incline to what they said, so they would incline to his speech and religion. "Idhan" is smoothness in what is not permitted, while mudarah is smoothness in what is permitted. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿so they would compromise﴾ is conjoined and is not an answer, for if it were an answer it would be in the accusative.

"Hallaf" is one who repeats his oath frequently. "Mahin" is weak of intellect and judgment, said by Mujahid, and it derives from "mahina" when he became weak; the mim is the first radical of the verb. Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "Mahin" is a liar.

"Hammaz" is one who attacks people. The root meaning of "hamz" in the language is striking with the hand, or with a stick or the like, and then it was borrowed for one who harms with his tongue. Mundhir said: and with his eye and his gesture. The hamzah (glottal stop) was so named because in uttering it there is sharpness and haste, so it was likened to striking with the hand. It was said to one of the Bedouins: "Do you strike the mouse?" He said: "The cat strikes it." It was said to another: "Do you strike Israel?" He said: "Then I would be a man of evil."

"Namim" is a verbal noun like "namimah" (tale-bearing), and it is conveying what one hears that causes harm and stirs up the souls. Hudhayfah related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No one who is a qattat (tale-carrier) will enter Paradise," and the qattat is the nammam. Many exegetes went to the view that these attributes are categories not intended for a particular man. Other groups said: rather it was revealed about a specific person, and this is disputed. Some said he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and his wealth supports this, and that he was the most famous of them for wealth and sons. Al-Shaʿbi and others said he is al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and this is supported by the fact that he had a growth on his throat like the wattle of a sheep, and also that he was from Thaqif, attached to the Quraysh. [p. 369] Ibn ʿAbbas, in the book of al-Tha'labi, said he is Abu Jahl. al-Naqqash mentioned ʿUtbah ibn Rabiʿah. Mujahid said he is al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth. The apparent wording is the generality of whoever has this attribute, and the address with this meaning continues through all time, especially for those in positions of authority.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 68, verse 12–20:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Hinderer of good, transgressor, sinful,﴾ ﴿brutal, and moreover of doubtful lineage.﴾ ﴿Because he possesses wealth and sons.﴾ ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Tales of the ancients!"﴾ ﴿We will brand him upon the snout.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the companions of the garden, when they swore that they would surely harvest its fruit in the morning,﴾ ﴿and did not make exception.﴾ ﴿Then there passed over it a visitation from your Lord while they were sleeping,﴾ ﴿so it became like the black-burnt night.﴾

Many of the exegetes said: "The good" here means wealth, so he is described as stingy. Others said: rather, it is general, covering wealth and righteous deeds; whoever is prevented from faith and obedience has been prevented from good. "Al-mu'tadi" is one who oversteps the limits of things. "Al-atheem" is a form (fa'il) derived from "al-ithm" (sin), in the sense of "athim" (sinful), because his deeds are ugly and earn sin.

"Al-'utull" is one strong of build, coarse of limbs, harsh of character, hard of heart, dull of understanding, a glutton and a heavy drinker who by night is a carcass and by day is a donkey. Whatever the exegetes have expressed of deficiencies of character issues from these qualities that were mentioned. It has been reported by al-Naqqash that the Prophet (ﷺ) explained "al-'utull" in a similar manner. These qualities are closely interrelated. Al-'utl means pushing with force, and from it comes "al-'atala" (crowbar). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿after that﴾ means: after what We have described him with. This ordering is only in the speech of the describer, not in the occurrence of those qualities in the one described; otherwise, his being "'utull" precedes his being one who withholds good.

"Al-zanim" in the speech of the Arabs is one attached to a people while not being of them. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, explained this verse with it. Murra al-Hamdani said: his father claimed him only after eighteen years, meaning the one about whom this verse was revealed. From this is the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"And you are a zanim, attached among the family of Hashim, as the single cup is hung behind the rider."

And also from it is the saying of Hassan:

"A zanim whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the stretched hide."

Many of the exegetes said: this is the intended meaning of the verse, because al-Akhnas ibn Shariq was from Thaqif, an ally of Quraysh. Ibn 'Abbas said: by "zanim" he meant that he had a zanama (wattle) on his neck like the zanama of a sheep, which is the piece of flesh hanging from its throat. We did not know the one referred to until this was revealed, so we recognized him by his wattle. Abu 'Ubayda said: a male goat is called zanim, since it has two wattles. From this is the saying of a Bedouin describing his goat: "As if its two wattles were the two udders of a she-camel of Qulays." It is also narrated that al-Akhnas ibn Shariq had this characteristic: he had a wattle. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also narrated that he said: when these attributes were revealed we did not know their possessor until "zanim" was revealed, and he was recognized by his wattle. Some exegetes said: "al-zanim" means one who is suspicious, of ugly deeds.

The recitation differed regarding His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿because he possesses wealth and sons﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and the people of Medina recited "an kana" as a declarative statement. Hamza recited "a-anna kana" with two hamzas, both lightened, as an interrogative. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited "ana kana" as an interrogative with the second hamza softened. The governing element of "an" is a hidden verb whose estimated form is: he disbelieved, or denied, or was obstinate. This verb is explained by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, to the end of the verse. It is permissible for the meaning to govern a word that comes later, since His saying "an kana" is in the position of an adverbial of time, as it can be estimated with "li" (for), i.e., "because he possessed." Some grammarians said that it is in a position of genitive by "li," as if it appeared; just as the meaning governs the preceding adverbial, so it governs this. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He will inform you when you are torn apart completely, that indeed you are in a new creation﴾ [Saba: 7]. The governing element of "idha" (when) is the meaning of His saying ﴿indeed you are in a new creation﴾ [Saba: 7], i.e., "you will be resurrected," or a similar estimate. It is not permissible for "yunabbi'u" to govern "idha," because it is a noun that is governed (by the clause), since "idha" has been made to be followed by a clause. Nor is it permissible for it to govern "an," as he said: because it is the answer to "idha," and an answer does not govern what precedes it.

Abu 'Ali permitted that "'utull" govern it, even though it has been described. On this analysis it is also correct that "zanim" govern it, especially according to the view of those who explain it as "one of ugly deeds." It is also permissible that "an kana" be governed by "tuti'uhu" (do not obey him), which is implied by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and do not obey﴾. This is far-fetched on the reading of the interrogative; rather, the meaning is only: "do not obey him because of his being such." For it, in every case, there is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi); reflect. The discussion of "al-asatir" (tales) has preceded in more than one place.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We will brand him upon the snout﴾, means: upon the nose, as said by al-Mubarrad. This is because "al-khurtum" is used metaphorically for the nose of a human being, while its true meaning is the snouts of beasts of prey. The threat in this verse is not that this person will be branded on his nose with a real mark; rather, this is an expression for an action resembling branding on the nose. People differed about that action. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is striking with the sword, i.e., he strikes him in the face and on his nose, so that it becomes like a brand on the nose, and that befell him on the day of Badr. Muhammad ibn Yazid al-Mubarrad said: it is in the punishment of the Hereafter in Hell, and it is torment with fire upon their noses. Others said: it is on the Day of Resurrection, i.e., he will be branded on his nose with a mark by which his disbelief and the abasement of his rank will be known. Qatada and others said: its meaning is that in this world He will do to him, by way of blame, disgrace, and public exposure of evil, what will remain on him and not be hidden from him; so that will be like a brand on the nose, firm and clear. This meaning is like your saying: "I will put a collar on you, the collar of the dove," meaning: I will establish the matter clearly upon you. Jarir intended this kind of meaning in his saying:

"When I placed my brand upon al-Farazdaq..."

Branding on the nose entails disfigurement, so its metaphorical use in dispraise has come to be most eloquent. If you reflect on the state of Abu Jahl and his like, and the bad reputation that was established for them in this world, you will see that they have indeed been branded on the snouts.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We tested them﴾, intends Quraysh, i.e., We put them to trial. "The companions of the garden," as is mentioned, were a group of brothers who had a father with a garden and a productive field; he would keep from it his own sustenance and give the rest in charity to the needy. It was said: rather, at harvest time he would bring the needy with him and feed them from it. Then the old man died, and his son said: "We are a group, and our father's conduct was an error. Let us go to our garden, and no needy person shall enter it against us, nor shall we give any of it." It is said: they plotted this matter and resolved upon it, so Allah sent a visitation by night, of fire or otherwise, and it burned. It was said: it became black, and it was said: white like harvested dry crops. When they awoke and went to their garden, they did not find it, so they supposed they had lost the way; then they recognized it and knew that Allah, Exalted is He, had struck them in it. They then repented and turned back, and they had been believers from among the People of the Book. Allah, Exalted is He, likened Quraysh to them in that He tested them with Muhammad (ﷺ) and guided them, as those had been tested through the deed of their father and through the commands of their law. Just as the punishment befell those in their garden, so it befalls these in all their worldly life. Then repentance is offered to whoever remains of them, as those repented. Many of the exegetes said: the seven years of drought that struck Quraysh are equivalent to what struck those in their garden.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that they would surely harvest it﴾: "li-yaslimunnaha" means "li-yajidunnaha" (that they would find it). "Sarram al-nakhl" is the cutting of its fruit, and likewise for every tree. "Musbihin" means: when they entered upon the morning. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿and did not make exception﴾ means: they did not hesitate in that, nor turn back from an opinion that prevented the needy. Mujahid said: its meaning is: they did not say "if Allah wills," but resolved upon that with the resolve of one who controls his affair. "Al-ta'if" is the matter that comes by night; al-Farra' mentioned this specification, and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿when a visitation of Satan touches them﴾ [al-A'raf: 201] refutes it. "Al-sarim": al-Farra', Munthir, and a group said: it means the night, because their bodies had turned black. Others said: it means the morning, because they had turned white like the harvested crop; this was said by Sufyan al-Thawri. "Al-sarim" is said of both the night and the day, because each of them is cut off (yanşarim) from the other. Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-sarim" is black ash in the dialect of Judhayma. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and others: al-sarim is a well-known sand-dune in Yemen that does not grow anything, and their bodies were likened to it.

And also from it is the saying of Hassan:

"A zanim whom men claimed as an addition, as the shanks are added to the stretched hide."

Many of the exegetes said: this is the intended meaning of the verse, because al-Akhnas ibn Shariq was from Thaqif, an ally of Quraysh. Ibn 'Abbas said: by "zanim" he meant that he had a zanama (wattle) on his neck like the zanama of a sheep, which is the piece of flesh hanging from its throat. We did not know the one referred to until this was revealed, so we recognized him by his wattle. Abu 'Ubayda said: a male goat is called zanim, since it has two wattles. From this is the saying of a Bedouin describing his goat: "As if its two wattles were the two udders of a she-camel of Qulays." Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, also narrated that he said: when these attributes were revealed we did not know their possessor until "zanim" was revealed, and he was recognized by his wattle. Some exegetes said: "al-zanim" means one who is suspicious, of ugly deeds.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and the people of Medina recited "an kana" as a declarative statement. Hamza recited "a-anna kana" with two hamzas, both lightened, as an interrogative. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited "ana kana" as an interrogative with the second hamza softened. This verb is explained by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, to the end of the verse. It is permissible for the meaning to govern a word that comes later, since His saying "an kana" is in the position of an adverbial of time, as it can be estimated with "li" (for), i.e., "because he possessed." Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, and the people of Medina recited "an kana" as a declarative statement. Hamza recited "a-anna kana" with two hamzas, both lightened, as an interrogative. Ibn 'Amir, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far recited "ana kana" as an interrogative with the second hamza softened. The governing element of "an" is a hidden verb whose estimated form is: he disbelieved, or denied, or was obstinate. This verb is explained by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, to the end of the verse. It is permissible for the meaning to govern a word that comes later, since His saying "an kana" is in the position of an adverbial of time, as it can be estimated with "li" (for), i.e., "because he possessed." Some grammarians said that it is in a position of genitive by "li," as if it appeared; just as the meaning governs the preceding adverbial, so it governs this. The governing element of "idha" (when) is the meaning of His saying ﴿indeed you are in a new creation﴾ [Saba: 7], i.e., "you will be resurrected," or a similar estimate. It is not permissible for "yunabbi'u" to govern "idha," because it is a noun that is governed (by the clause), since "idha" has been made to be followed by a clause. Nor is it permissible for it to govern "an," as he said: because it is the answer to "idha," and an answer does not govern what precedes it.

Abu 'Ali permitted that "'utull" govern it, even though it has been described. On this analysis it is also correct that "zanim" govern it, especially according to the view of those who explain it as "one of ugly deeds." It is also permissible that "an kana" be governed by "tuti'uhu" (do not obey him), which is implied by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and do not obey﴾. This is far-fetched on the reading of the interrogative; rather, the meaning is only: "do not obey him because of his being such." For it, in every case, there is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi); reflect. The discussion of "al-asatir" (tales) has preceded in more than one place.

This is because "al-khurtum" is used metaphorically for the nose of a human being, while its true meaning is the snouts of beasts of prey. People differed about that action. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is striking with the sword, i.e., he strikes him in the face and on his nose, so that it becomes like a brand on the nose, and that befell him on the day of Badr. Qatada and others said: its meaning is that in this world He will do to him, by way of blame, disgrace, and public exposure of evil, what will remain on him and not be hidden from him; so that will be like a brand on the nose, firm and clear. "When I placed my brand upon al-Farazdaq..."

Branding on the nose entails disfigurement, so its metaphorical use in dispraise has come to be most eloquent. If you reflect on the state of Abu Jahl and his like, and the bad reputation that was established for them in this world, you will see that they have indeed been branded on the snouts.

"The companions of the garden," as is mentioned, were a group of brothers who had a father with a garden and a productive field; he would keep from it his own sustenance and give the rest in charity to the needy. It was said: rather, at harvest time he would bring the needy with him and feed them from it. Then the old man died, and his son said: "We are a group, and our father's conduct was an error. It is said: they plotted this matter and resolved upon it, so Allah sent a visitation by night, of fire or otherwise, and it burned. It was said: it became black, and it was said: white like harvested dry crops. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 68, verse 21–29:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So they called out to one another in the morning,﴾ ﴿"Go early to your field, if you intend to harvest."﴾ ﴿So they set off, speaking in low voices,﴾ ﴿"Let no needy person enter it today against you."﴾ ﴿And they went early, with determination.﴾ ﴿But when they saw it, they said, "Indeed, we have gone astray."﴾ ﴿"Rather, we have been deprived."﴾ ﴿The most moderate of them said, "Did I not tell you, 'Why do you not glorify Allah?'"﴾ ﴿They said, "Glory be to our Lord! Indeed, we were wrongdoers."﴾

"Tanadaw" (they called to one another) means: some of them urged one another to proceed to their appointed time. Some of the Seven Readers read "an-ughdu" (أنِ اغْدُوا) with a dammah on the nun, and others with a kasrah; this has been discussed many times before. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿if you intend to harvest (ṣārimīn)﴾, may mean [harvesting] from "ṣirām an-nakhl" (cutting of palm dates), and it may mean: if you are people of resolve and determination in your opinion, from your saying "a sharp sword" (sayf ṣārim).

"Yatakhāfatūn" (speaking in low voices) means: they speak a quiet speech, and from it is the saying of the Exalted, ﴿and do not speak in a low voice therein﴾. This whispering was out of fear that the needy would perceive them, and the words they whispered were ﴿let no needy person enter it today against you.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "lā yadkhulannahā" (لا يَدْخُلَنَّها) without "an" (أنْ).

The saying of the Exalted, "ʿalā ḥard" (with determination), may mean: "ʿalā man'" (with prevention), from their saying: "ḥāradat al-ibil" (the camels withheld) when their milk diminished and they withheld it, and "ḥāradat as-sanah" (the year became barren) when it was a dry year with no produce. From it is the saying of the poet:

"And the stingy, stern ones withheld, and there was no return for the lending of the borrowers' pots."

It may also mean "al-qaṣd" (intention), and some philologists explained it thus and recited as evidence:

"A torrent came from the presence of Allah, *** heading toward the garden that was walled in."

That is: it sets out its intent. It may also mean "al-ghaḍab" (anger); it is said: "ḥarada ar-rajul yaḥridu ḥardan" (the man became angry) when he was enraged, and from it is the saying of al-Ashhab ibn Rumaylah:

"Lions of Sharā met hidden lions, *** they gave one another drink in anger over the blood of the lions."

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿capable (qādirīn)﴾, may be from "al-qudrah" (power), that is: they were capable in their own estimation; and it may be from "at-taqdīr" (determining), as if they had determined to act against the needy, that is, they constrained them. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and whoever has his provision restricted﴾ [al-Talaq: 7]. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿but when they saw it﴾, meaning burned, they thought they had lost the way and that it was not that [garden]; but when they realized it, they knew that it had been struck. So they said, "Rather, we have been deprived," meaning: we have been deprived of its produce and its blessing. Then the most just of them in speech, intellect and character, who was the most moderate (awsaṭ), said to them. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿a moderate community﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning: just and excellent. As for "tusabbiḥūn" (you glorify), it was said it is an expression for obeying Allah the Exalted, exalting Him, and acting in obedience to Him; and Mujahid and Abu Salih said it was for them the expression of exception (al-istithna').

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is refuted by their saying, "Glory be to our Lord." So the people hastened at that point, repented at that point, glorified Allah, and acknowledged their wrongdoing in their belief in withholding from the poor.

This is refuted by their saying, "Glory be to our Lord." So the people hastened at that point, repented at that point, glorified Allah, and acknowledged their wrongdoing in their belief in withholding from the poor.

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, binding until the Day of Resurrection, that you shall have whatever you decide?﴾ ﴿Ask them which of them stands surety for that.﴾ ﴿Or do they have partners? Then let them bring their partners, if they are truthful.﴾ ﴿On the day when the shin is uncovered and they are called to prostration, but they will not be able to.﴾ ﴿Their eyes downcast, humiliation covering them, though they were called to prostration while they were sound.﴾ ﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this discourse. We will draw them on gradually from where they do not know.﴾ ﴿And I will give them respite. Indeed, My plan is firm.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, binding until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is addressed to the disbelievers, as if He were saying: Have We sworn to you an oath that constitutes a covenant with you that We will bestow favour upon you on the Day of Resurrection and beyond it?

The majority of the reciters read *bāligha* (binding) in the nominative, as an adjective of *aymān* (oaths). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read *bāligatan* in the accusative, as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl). It is a ḥāl from an indefinite noun specified by His saying *'alaynā* (from Us). Al-A'raj read *a-inna lakum* (with the interrogative hamza), and likewise in His saying in the earlier passage: ﴿Indeed, for you therein is what you choose﴾ [al-Qalam: 38].

Then God commanded Muhammad (ﷺ), as a means of establishing proof against them, to ask them who it is that stands as surety (*zaʿīm*) for them in this matter. The *zaʿīm* is the one who guarantees the matter and undertakes it.

Then God caused them to stand before the matter of the partners, perhaps they would suppose that these could benefit them in any of this. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abi 'Abla read *am lahum shirkun fa-l-yaʾtū bi-shirkihim* with a kasra on the *shīn* and without an *alif*. The meaning in both readings is the idols. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿then let them bring their partners﴾ — it has been said that this is a summons and a causing to stand in this world, meaning: let them bring them so that We may see whether they are of the sort that harms and benefits or not. It has also been said that it is a summons and a causing to stand so that they bring them on the Day of Resurrection, the day when the shin is uncovered.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿the day when the shin is uncovered﴾. Mujahid said: it is the first hour of the Resurrection, and it is the most terrifying of its hours. There is a supporting report from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A caller will call out on the Day of Resurrection: let every person follow what they used to worship. He said: So whoever used to worship the sun follows the sun, whoever used to worship the moon follows the moon, and likewise every worshipper follows every object of worship. Then this community and the remnant of the People of the Book remain with them, along with their hypocrites and many of the disbelievers. It will be said to them: What is your condition? Why do you stay while the people have gone? They will say: We are waiting for our Lord. He said: Then God will come to them in other than the form in which they recognised Him, and He will say: I am your Lord. They will say: We seek refuge in God from You. He said: Then He will say: Do you recognise Him by a sign you see? They will say: Yes. Then He will uncover the shin for them, and they will say: Yes, You are our Lord, and they will fall down in prostration. Every believer will prostrate, while the backs of the hypocrites and the disbelievers will turn into a single bone like the cow's vertebrae, so they will not be able to prostrate."

Thus is the hadith, although some of its wording differs by addition and omission. In every form of what I have mentioned, the uncovering of the shin is related, and what appears in the verse of this also: it is merely an expression of the intensity of the terror and the greatness of the power which God displays on that day, until knowledge is established that such power belongs to God alone. From this meaning is the saying of the poet describing war:

*She has uncovered for them her shin, and the open field of evil has appeared.*

And from it is the saying of another:

*She has rolled up her shin, so hold fast.*

And the saying of another:

*In a year that has uncovered its shin,
red, stripping the flesh from its bones.*

The root of this is that whoever wishes to exert earnest effort in a matter he is undertaking uncovers his shin, as a sign of rolling up and seriousness. Poets have praised this meaning, and from it is the saying of Durayd:

*Tight of waist-cloth, with half his shin showing,
patient against enemies, a leaper upon the high ground.*

On this basis, whoever wishes earnest effort and resolve in obedience to God, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, peace and blessings be upon him: "The waist-wrap of the believer reaches to the middle of the shin."

The majority of people read *yukshafu* with a *ḍamma* on the *yāʾ*, in the passive form of the verb. Ibn Mas'ud read *yakshifu* with a *fatḥa* on the *yāʾ* and a kasra on the *shīn*, meaning: God uncovers. Ibn 'Abbas read *takshifu* with a *fatḥa* on the *tāʾ*, meaning that the Resurrection is the one that uncovers. Ibn 'Abbas also read *tukshafu* with a *ḍamma* on the *tāʾ*, meaning: the Resurrection and the severe present state are uncovered. Al-Akhfash reported from him that he read *nakshifu* with an *nūn* open and a kasra on the *shīn*, and it is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they are called﴾. Its apparent meaning is that there is a summons to prostration there. This is refuted by what has been established in the Law, that the Hereafter is not a place of action and that there is no obligation in it. If that is so, then the one summoning is what they see of the believers' prostration, so they wish to prostrate at that time, but they are not able. Some scholars have held that they are called to prostration by way of rebuke. Some people have drawn from His saying, ﴿so they are not able﴾, that they were able before that, but that does not necessarily follow. The creed of the Ash'ariyya (the followers of al-Ash'ari) is that *istitāʿa* (capacity to act) exists only together with the act itself, not before it, and this much is sufficient on this question here.

*Khāshiʿatan* (downcast) is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. All their limbs are downcast, meaning humbled, but God singled out the eyes for mention because humility is more evident in them than in any other limb. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿humiliation covering them﴾ means: it disturbs their souls and appears upon them in a manner that disgraces them. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿though they were called to prostration﴾ means, in the abode of this world, while they were sound from what befell the bones of their backs through arrogance and rebellion. Some of the exegetes said: prostration here is an expression for all acts of obedience, and prostration was singled out for mention because it is the greatest of acts of obedience, and because by it they were tested in the Hereafter. Ibrahim al-Taymi and al-Sha'bi said: by prostration is meant the obligatory prayers. Ibn Jubayr said: the meaning is that they used to hear the call to prayer and "hasten to success" (ḥayya ʿalā al-falāḥ) and would not respond. Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham became paralysed, so he was led between two men to the mosque. It was said to him: you are truly excused. He said: whoever hears "hasten to success" let him respond, even if he has to crawl. It was said to Ibn al-Musayyab: Tariq wants to kill you, so sit in your house. He said: I hear "hasten to success" and do not respond? By God, I shall not do that. All of this is close, some of it to others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So leave Me with whoever denies this discourse﴾ is a threat. There was no obstacle there, but it is like when you say: "Leave me with so-and-so," meaning: I shall punish him. *Man* (whoever) is in the accusative position, either as a conjunction with the pronoun in *dhurnī* (leave me), or accusative as an object with (*maʿa*, together with). The *ḥadīth* referred to is the Qur'an that reports these unseen matters. *Istidrāj* (drawing on gradually) is the carrying of a person from one rank to another until the one carried reaches evil. *Istidrāj* is used only for evil, and it is derived from *darj* (a step). Sufyan al-Thawri said: they are showered with blessings and refuse thankfulness. Others said: whenever they increase in sin, they are increased in blessing. Among the meanings of *istidrāj* is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "God, exalted is He, gives respite to the wrongdoer until, when He seizes him, He does not let him go." Al-Hasan said: how many are drawn on gradually by kindness shown to them, and deceived by being concealed.

*Umlī lahum* means: I delay them for a measured period of time, which is a span and a portion. It is said *mulāwa*, with a *ḍamma*, *fatḥa* or kasra on the *mīm*. *Al-kayd* (plan) is an expression for the punishment that befalls the disbelievers, in that it is a plan on their part, so the punishment is named by the name of the sin. *Al-matīn* (firm) means the strong one who has firmness, and from it comes *al-matn* (the back, spine).

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Or do you have oaths from Us, binding until the Day of Resurrection, that you shall have whatever you decide?﴾ ﴿Ask them which of them stands surety for that.﴾ ﴿Or do they have partners? This "am" (or, a particle used here to mean "rather") is the one that implies a turning away from the previous speech, not in the sense of rejecting it, but in the sense of leaving it and turning to something else. This questioning is addressed to Muhammad (ﷺ), and its purpose is to rebuke the disbelievers. Then the Exalted commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient with His judgment, and to proceed with what he was commanded of conveying the message and bearing harm and hardship. He forbade him from the impatience and haste into which Yunus (peace be upon him) fell. Then the Exalted mentioned the story concisely, and mentioned what happened at its end, namely his calling out from the belly of the fish while he was ﴿suppressing [his grief]﴾, that is, his anger was held in his chest. The real meaning of "al-kazm" (suppressing, restraining) is anger, grief and regret, and the one who suppresses is described by it figuratively, though in reality he is the one who restrains. A similar usage is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"And you, from love of Mayy, conceal a grief, the heart of you troubled, wounded, and suppressed."

Al-Naqqash said: al-makzum is the one whose throat (kazm) has been seized, and it is the passage of the heart. From this the "al-kazimah" was named, which is the conduit in the depths of the earth.

Most reciters read: ﴿Had it not been that a blessing from his Lord had overtaken him﴾, attributing the verb without a feminine marker, because the feminine form of "ni'mah" (blessing) is not real. Ibn Hurmuz read: "tadarakahu" with a doubled dal, meaning "tatadarakahu" (she would overtake him). This is a depiction of a state that is coming, which is why the verb came in the non-past form, in the sense of: had it not been that it would be said about him, "a blessing from his Lord overtakes him." A similar usage is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and he found in it two men fighting﴾. This is the explanation of this reading, and then the "ta'" was assimilated into the "dal" (idgham, merging of one consonant into another). The "ara'" (open wasteland) is the wide earth in which there is nothing that covers anything, whether building, plants, or other things such as a mountain or the like. From it is the saying of the poet:

"So I raised a foot whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast my garments onto the open ground."

Yunus (peace be upon him) was indeed cast onto the open ground, while not being blameworthy. "Ijtaba-hu" means: he chose him and selected him.

The majority of reciters read: ﴿la-yuzliqunaka﴾ with a damma on the ya', from "azlaqa" (to cause to slip). Nafi' alone read: ﴿la-yazliqunaka﴾ with a fatha on the ya', from "zalaqat al-rijl" (the foot slipped). It is said: "zaliqat al-rijl" (with a kasra on the lam) and "zalaqatu-hu" (with a fatha), like "hazana" and "hazanat-hu" (to grieve, to cause grief), and "shatarat al-'ayn" and "shatarat-ha" (the eye squinted, to cause it to squint). So all praise is due to Allah, who has bestowed His favour upon us through it, and made us its people and its bearers. There is no lord but Him.

The commentary on Surah [al-Qalam] is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
